newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock mutual fund flood not seen sustainable.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock mutual fund flood not seen sustainable.

text.p: A recent tide of new money into stock mutual funds stirred hopes that individuals are storming back to Wall Street, but analysts cautioned that a $20 billion monthly pace is not sustainable.

The Investment Company Institute on Wednesday estimated new investments in stock funds at $19.0 billion, up sharply from July's $5.8 billion and June's $14.46 billion. From January to May 1996 monthly money flows topped $20 billion.
"Hallelujah!" enthused Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer of Gruntal & Co.
"There's no question there's an ongoing movement of money into retirement and forced savings. There's great liquidity on the buyside...The economy and Fed are doing their part."
But he agreed a $20 billion monthly flow is unsustainable.
"We'll see an erratic pattern with market volatility. One month it diminishes and then the next month, a ramping up."

Indeed the early July correction that wiped 10 percent off the Dow industrials and 20 percent off the Nasdaq Composite unnerved some professionals and sent many individual investors fleeing. Signs of a strong economy, inflation and rate fears and corporate earnings warnings fuelled the stiff selling.

But the subsequent steadiness in markets and the return of the closely-watched Dow to near record territory has apparently again sent the siren call of stocks to some investors. The Dow on Wednesday rose 28 to 5754.92, shy of May 22's 5778.00 record closing high.
"I'm still telling people to be cautious. We don't put too much emphasis on the ICI data and it is a lagging indicator," said Harry Laubscher, a Tucker Anthony market analyst.
Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest, sees choppy stock action through mid-October amid the corporate earnings preannouncements period.
Actual third-quarter earnings reports, "will click in and be the final catalyst to get this market to new highs."
Battipaglia still sees a Dow 6000 by year-end. "But it won't lift all boats. There may be a focus on big S&P 500 names and secondary and tertiary" stocks may lag.
Analysts said the September 24 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, where a modest tightening may be announced and the historically weak October month were near-term hurdles.
But they noted equities remain an attractive long-term investment for aging baby boomers.
"Stocks are the only game in town. The only place for a decent return. Equities' return year-to-date is much better than bonds or real estate," Shaughnessy said.
